ous red-naked galaxy, ESO 320-G004, have been analyzed to determine the cause of its enigmatic nature. Models suggest that the galaxy consists of a luminous bulge surrounded by a star-forming system of blue dwarf galaxies. Images indicate that the perceived thin appearance of ESO 320-G004 is an illusion created by overlapping galaxy planes, one of which is heavily obscured. A reddened filament extending from the bulge supports this theory, implying that the prominent red color arises from dust absorption rather than intrinsic galaxy properties. Photometric observations reveal that the filament's optical brightness surpasses that of typical tidal tails, suggesting they might be related. Spectra obtained from the bulge and the filament resemble those of blue dwarf galaxies, except the filament exhibits stronger Balmer lines and a more pronounced absorption at 430 nm, indicative of the interplay between stellar and atomic processes in the redshifted gas. A possible explanation for the blue stellar lines is the ionization and ionization feedback effect exerting pressure on the surrounding He I cloud, causing the gas to cool and condense as it travels along the filament, possibly giving rise to the observed interplay of matter and radiation in the system. Balmer absorption could also be the result of the interaction between stars and gas within isolated star clusters, which might shed more light on the mysterious nature of the red-naked galaxies, a class of objects comprising ESO 320-G004 and its counterparts in the local universe. This paper presents a geometric representation of a continuous-time Markov chain model for these networks, dividing the state space into distinct categories based on network topology and using a boundary partition to describe transitions between these blocks. We then establish an asymptotic curve that estimates an exponential convergence rate towards stable network topologies in this model. This work specifically explores its applicability to birth-death and resource allocation processes. We further provide an updated version of the theory initially presented in a landmark study by Nekovee et al. in 2003. Although the theory in that study shares similarities with the one presented here, it lacks the boundary partition and the associated geometric representation. For instance, the theory in that study indicates that for birth-death processes, the state space falls into the category of monopartite networks consisting of either a single connected component or components separated by a limited number of edges. Conversely, the theory in this study reveals that for birth-death processes, the state space falls into the category of either monopartite networks consisting of at most two connected components separated by a limited number of edges, or bipartite networks consisting of two identical components separated by a limited number of edges. This distinction brings about a significant change in description which implies that bipartite networks cannot be reached from monopartite ones. As a result, the state at which the process stops can be determined earlier and with greater precision in the geometric representation model in comparison to the traditional Markov chain model. For instance, the time required for the process to stop can be bounded from both above and below in the geometric representation model in contrast to the traditional Markov chain model which only permits upper bounding. For various birth-death processes, the geometric representation model is capable of calculating exact transition times between various states, which in turn can be used to update and refresh the boundaries in the geometric representation model, thereby allowing for computations of long-term behavior in the geometric representation model. This is in contrast to the traditional Markov chain model which lacks methods for computing long-term behavior. As a result, the geometric representation model is capable of delivering solution sets of varying sizes, which in turn can be used to compute the exact mean first hitting times for reaching bipartite networks from monopartite ones. This is in contrast to the traditional model which lacks such information and is only capable of providing an upper bound on the mean first hitting times for reaching bipartite networks from monopartite ones. A major drawback of the traditional approach remains the need to manually set a threshold to balance accuracy and system cost. This paper proposes a groundbreaking, label-and-rankagnostic method called Self-Supervised Re-identification Network (SSRN). SSRN starts by developing a self-supervised model via an end-to-end process for comparing identity images. This model uses two approaches:  a ranking-based method and subspace analysis, to automatically and uniformly determine the similarity threshold. Initially, the model pairs images with similar identities and contrasts them with those of unrelated individuals. This sets the baseline for comparing identity images. Next, the model uses subspace analysis to identify the most distinguishing factors in the paired images and demarcates a boundary to separate identical identities. This ranking-based method offers an alternative approach to set the threshold, by examining the order of pairs with the same identity. This method outperforms existing ReID models and justifies the effectiveness of human face recognition systems. SSRN's innovative approach constitutes a new paradigm in the Self-Supervised Re-identification Networks, as the only one of its kind. It lays the groundwork for a new future of fully automatic identity matching with no need for human intervention. SSRN's complete source code is available at: https://github.com/HJJ-jack/SSRN.
